say.text: Two ulcers on the first part of the duodenum. One sits on the front wall, one on the back wall.
Which one is the one that perforates?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Not right. The back wall feels like the deep, dangerous site, so the back-wall ulcer is tempting.
But a back-wall duodenal ulcer usually bleeds, eroding the gastroduodenal artery. The front wall is the one that perforates.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the back wall bleeds, the front wall perforates.

say.text: Ask which wall faces the open peritoneal cavity once an ulcer erodes through it.
Yes. Here is patient A, worked in full: sudden epigastric pain, and a front-wall ulcer on the first part of the duodenum.
Step 1: the ulcer erodes through the whole wall into the free peritoneal cavity. That is a perforation.
Step 2: gut acid, bile and enzymes spill out first, causing chemical peritonitis.
Step 3: the exudate dilutes that irritant, so he feels better for a while. This is the period of reaction, and it can mislead you.
Step 4: bacteria contaminate the fluid over hours, and the picture becomes bacterial peritonitis.
Patient B: same first part of the duodenum, but the ulcer is on the back wall. He vomits blood and passes black stools.
Steps 1 and 2 are done for you: this one bleeds. Which artery was eroded?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The posterior duodenal ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery, so it bleeds instead of perforating.
Not right. The left gastric is the stomach's own big artery, so a gastric-looking source is tempting.
But this ulcer sits on the first part of the duodenum. A posterior duodenal ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the artery: the duodenal ulcer bleeds from the gastroduodenal artery.

say.text: Not right. The splenic artery is a big named vessel in the upper abdomen, so it looks plausible for an upper bleed.
But a posterior duodenal ulcer bleeds from the gastroduodenal artery, the vessel that sits right beside this segment.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the vessel: the duodenal bleed comes from the gastroduodenal artery.

say.text: Which artery lies closest to the first part of the duodenum itself?
Six hours on from patient A's perforation. The pain has eased and he looks more comfortable, though the abdomen is still tender.
What does this mean?

choices.label: Recovery: observe and re-examine him in the morning
Spontaneous sealing: discharge on a PPI tonight
Reaction phase: the irritant is diluted, bacteria follow
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. This is the period of reaction: exudate dilutes the irritant, so he feels better while bacterial peritonitis builds.
Not right. Feeling better is the reassuring sign, so a settling patient looks like a recovering one.
But the relief is the reaction stage, which misleads. The infection is still building behind it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this: the improvement is the lull before bacterial peritonitis.

say.text: Not right. A sealed perforation is walled off by organs, so a quieter abdomen can look sealed.
This one is still a free leak with a tender abdomen. The lull is the reaction phase, not sealing.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the word: sealed means walled off, and this leak is still open.

say.text: Ask what the exudate does to the irritant, and what that does to how he feels.
What is the right order of the three classic stages after a perforation?

choices.label: Reaction, then chemical peritonitis, then bacterial peritonitis
Chemical peritonitis, then reaction, then bacterial peritonitis
Bacterial peritonitis, then reaction, then chemical peritonitis

say.text: Yes. Chemical first, then the reaction phase, then diffuse bacterial peritonitis.
Not right. The reaction stage is the calm that looks like a start, so it is tempting to put it first.
But the acid spill comes first, causing chemical peritonitis. The reaction follows as the exudate dilutes it.
Not right. Bacteria feel like the cause of everything, so it is tempting to start the course there.
Bacteria arrive later, over hours, after the chemical spill and the reaction stage.
Two patients with severe abdominal pain. One lies motionless with a rigid abdomen. The other keeps rolling and pacing.
Which one has peritonitis?

choices.label: The patient who keeps rolling and pacing

say.text: Yes. Peritonitis lies still, because movement hurts the inflamed peritoneum; the rigid abdomen fits.
Not right. The pacing patient looks more distressed, so restlessness seems like the peritonitis picture.
Colic is the restless one: movement eases it. Peritonitis keeps still, because movement hurts.
Why does the peritonitis patient lie still while the colic patient writhes?

choices.label: Movement is blocked by pain in the gut wall, as in colic
Movement jars the inflamed peritoneum and worsens pain
Severe pain always makes a patient move about

say.text: Yes. Inflamed peritoneum is jarred by movement, so the patient keeps still. Colic gut eases with movement.
Not right. Pain in the gut wall sounds like colic, so a cramp-like picture seems to explain the stillness.
Colic patients move because movement eases them. Peritonitis hurts with movement, so they stay still.
Not right. Severe pain feels like it should drive movement, so pain severity is tempting as the reason.
Pain size does not set the movement sign. Movement itself hurts in peritonitis, so the patient stays still.
